name: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
summary: How agents loop, call tools, delegate to subagents and keep state. The exam asks where control should live: in the model's judgement, or in code that enforces it.
keyIdeas: The agentic loop continues while stop_reason is "tool_use" and ends on "end_turn"; tool results go back into the conversation so the model can plan the next step.
Coordinator-subagent (hub and spoke): the coordinator decomposes, delegates, and merges. Subagents have isolated context and receive only what the coordinator passes in their prompt.
Independent subagent calls can be issued in parallel in one coordinator turn; sequential calls only where one result feeds the next.
Prompts are probabilistic. When a rule has financial, legal or safety consequences, enforce it in code: hooks, prerequisite gates, programmatic checks.
Fixed prompt chains suit predictable multi-step work; dynamic decomposition suits open-ended investigation.
Sessions can be resumed or forked; after code changed on disk, tell the agent which files changed or start fresh with a summary.
Escalate to a human with a structured handoff: the human cannot see the transcript.
traps: Parsing the model's prose to decide whether the loop is finished.
Using an iteration cap as the main stopping condition instead of a backstop.
Assuming a subagent automatically inherits the coordinator's history.
Enforcing a high-stakes rule only with a stronger prompt.

name: Tool Design & MCP Integration
summary: How Claude picks tools and how tools should answer. Tool descriptions are the selection mechanism; structured errors and scoped tool sets keep agents reliable.
keyIdeas: The tool description is what Claude uses to choose: state purpose, input formats, examples, and boundaries against similar tools.
Return structured errors (isError, error category, retryable flag). A valid empty result is not a failure and must look different from one.
Give each agent a small, scoped tool set (roughly 4-5). Eighteen tools on one agent degrade selection.
tool_choice: "auto" lets the model decide, "any" forces some tool call, and a named tool forces that tool.
Project MCP servers go in .mcp.json (shared in version control, secrets via ${ENV_VAR}); personal or experimental ones go in user config.
MCP resources expose catalogues (issue lists, doc trees) so the model needn't explore with repeated tool calls.
Built-ins: Grep searches file contents, Glob matches file names, Edit changes text at a unique anchor, Read plus Write is the fallback.
traps: Fixing misrouting by adding system-prompt rules instead of improving tool descriptions.
Returning "Operation failed" with no category.
Treating an empty search result as an error and retrying forever.
Committing a token inside .mcp.json.

name: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
summary: Configuring Claude Code for a team and running it safely in pipelines: memory files, scoped rules, commands and skills, hooks, permissions, plan mode and CI.
keyIdeas: CLAUDE.md levels: user (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, personal), project (shared via git), and directory-level for local conventions. Use @imports to keep files modular and /memory to see what loaded.
.claude/rules/*.md with a paths: glob in frontmatter applies a convention to matching files wherever they live.
Project slash commands live in .claude/commands (shared); personal ones in ~/.claude/commands. Skills (SKILL.md) can run with context: fork to keep their output out of the main context.
Hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse…) enforce behaviour deterministically; CLAUDE.md instructions are advisory.
Plan mode for multi-file, multi-approach changes; direct execution for small, well-defined ones.
CI: run non-interactively with -p, use --output-format json (optionally with a JSON schema) and give the job its context in CLAUDE.md.
Message Batches API is about 50% cheaper but has up to a 24-hour window and no latency guarantee: fine for overnight work, wrong for blocking checks.
A fresh, independent session reviews better than the session that wrote the code.
traps: Putting team conventions in the user-level file so new teammates never get them.
Using Batches for a pre-merge gate.
Asking the same session to review its own work.
Relying on a CLAUDE.md sentence to guarantee a security rule.

name: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
summary: Writing prompts that behave in production and getting machine-readable output you can trust: explicit criteria, few-shot examples, schemas, validation and retry loops.
keyIdeas: Explicit criteria ("flag only when the comment contradicts the code") beat vague guidance ("be conservative").
A noisy category destroys trust; disable it while you refine its criteria.
Two to four targeted few-shot examples, with the reasoning, fix ambiguous cases and format drift.
Tool use with a JSON schema removes syntax errors but not semantic ones (wrong field, totals that don't add up).
Make fields nullable or optional when the source may not contain them; add "other" or "unclear" enum values with a detail field.
Retry with the original document, the failed output and the specific validation error. Retrying cannot recover information that is not in the source.
Extract both a stated and a calculated total to detect inconsistencies.
Review in passes: per-file local passes plus a cross-file integration pass beats one huge pass.
traps: Believing a schema guarantees correct values.
Making every field required so the model invents values.
Retrying when the document simply lacks the data.
Adding "be accurate" and calling it criteria.

name: Context Management & Reliability
summary: Keeping long and multi-agent work accurate: what to preserve, when to escalate, how errors travel between agents, how to sample for human review, and how to keep provenance.
keyIdeas: Progressive summarisation drops numbers, dates and IDs. Keep a persistent case-facts block outside the summarised history.
Put key findings at the start or end of long inputs and trim bulky tool output to the fields that matter.
Honour an explicit request for a human immediately. Escalate on policy gaps or lack of progress, not on sentiment scores or the model's self-rated confidence.
Ask for another identifier when several records match instead of guessing.
Propagate structured failure context (type, attempt, partial results, alternatives); never turn a failure into an empty success, and don't abort everything for one failure.
For large codebases: scratchpad files, subagents for specific questions, /compact, and a manifest for crash recovery.
Aggregate accuracy hides weak segments: sample by confidence and by segment, and calibrate on labelled data.
Keep claim-to-source mappings and dates; when sources conflict, show both with attribution.
traps: Choosing the higher number when two sources disagree.
Using sentiment as the escalation trigger.
Swallowing a subagent error and returning no results.
Trusting a 97% overall score without segment breakdown.
